prompt: Discuss Aristotle's account of phantasia and its role in practical reasoning, drawing on De Anima III.3 and the relevant commentators.

# Phantasia and Practical Reasoning in Aristotle's De Anima III.3 

## 1. Phantasia and Aisthesis Aristotle's account of φαντασία occupies a critical juncture between his treatment of sensation and his investigation of νοῦς, such that the image-making faculty emerges precisely where perception alone proves insufficient full range of psychic activity. sight or seeing: imagination takes place in the absence of both, as e.g. in dreams" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 41–43). This passage establishes the fundamental contrast between φαντασία and αἴσθησις: whereas perception requires the actual presence of an external sensible object and the corresponding activation of a sensory organ, phantasia operates even when the perceiver is no longer in contact with the perceptible thing, as in dreaming or recollection. The distinction is not merely one of temporal occasion; it is, rather, a distinction in the mode of psychic movement involved. Phantasia, understood as a κίνησις arising from the actuality of sensation, retains the formal character of perceptual content while becoming functionally autonomous from the conditions that originally produced it (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 15–16). Indeed, Caston emphasizes that phantasia can be false, noting that Aristotle treats scene-paintings and dreams as cases in which something is produced that is "not what they produce a phantasia of" (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 15–16). This capacity for error is precisely what differentiates phantasia from veridical perception of proper sensibles; accordingly, phantasia supplies a form of intentionality that makes error possible where perception alone could not account for it (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, p. 18). The grades of phantasia—sensory (αἰσθητική) and deliberative (βουλευτική)—will be examined in greater detail in the sections that follow; here it suffices even at its most elementary, phantasia is grounded in the prior operation of sense-perception while exceeding its scope. 

## 2. Phantasma and Phantasia The relationship between φαντασία as a capacity and φάντασμα as its product constitutes one of the most consequential conceptual dependencies in Aristotle's psychology. The phantasma is the quasi-perceptual content that persists after the cessation of actual sensation, serving as the medium through which the thinking soul engages its objects. (Aristotle 2014, *Movement Of Animals*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]), "to the thinking soul images serve as if they were contents of perception (and when it asserts or denies them to be good or bad it avoids or pursues them)" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 47–48). This passage reveals that the phantasma functions not merely as a residual trace of perception but as the operative material upon which practical and theoretical thought alike depend; the soul never thinks without a phantasma, and it is through the phantasma that the desirable or the fearful is presented to the agent. Hence the phantasma mediates between the sensory particular and the universal judgment, providing the content upon which deliberative phantasia—the higher grade of imagination available to rational animals—can operate. In the *Movement of Animals*, Aristotle confirms this mediating role when "thinking and imagination, as we said above, produce that which brings about the affections, since they produce the forms which bring them about" (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, p. 11). The phantasma thus carries a form analogous to the perceptual form received in sensation, yet it does so independently of the external object's presence; this independence is what permits the voluntariness characteristic of deliberative phantasia, in which the agent can summon and arrange images before the mind's eye. Burke, reading the broader rhetorical tradition, similarly recognizes imagination's mediating power when classical dictum to "recommend the dictates of reason to imagination, in order to excite the appetite and will" (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 93–96). The phantasma is thus both product and instrument of phantasia's distinctive movement. 

## 3. Phantasia and Mneme The contrast between φαντασία and μνήμη illuminates a further dimension of the image's psychic life, for memory necessarily involves a temporal index that phantasia as such does not require. (Aristotle 2014, *Movement Of Animals*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) in *On Memory*, "all memory, therefore, implies a time elapsed; consequently only those animals which perceive time remember, and the organ whereby they perceive time is also that whereby they remember" (Aristotle, *On Memory*, p. 1). Memory thus presupposes both phantasia and the perception of temporal magnitude; the phantasma that serves memory must be apprehended not merely as an image of something but as an image belonging to a determinate past. Phantasia, by contrast, can present its content as though temporally unmoored—as in dreams or in the voluntary summoning of images during deliberation—without thereby constituting an act of recollection. This distinction bears directly on the grades of phantasia, for deliberative phantasia involves the construction and comparison of future-directed images rather than the recovery of past-directed ones; it is accordingly oriented toward the prospective good rather than the elapsed event (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 23). The relation between phantasia and memory also highlights the tension identified in the corpus: phantasia's causal derivation from sensation coexists with its functional autonomy in domains such as memory retention, where the phantasma persists as a likeness of the absent object and simultaneously as a record of a past encounter. 5), a vulnerability that extends to mnemonic phantasmata no less than to perceptual ones. 

## 4. Phantasia and Doxa The relationship between φαντασία and δόξα requires careful delineation, for Aristotle is at pains imagination is neither identical with nor reducible to belief. possibility of doxa insofar as opinion depends upon the presentation of content that can be affirmed or denied; yet phantasia itself involves no propositional commitment. Animals that possess sensory phantasia but lack λόγος can respond to images without forming beliefs in the strict sense, thus confirming the interpretive bridge: some non-rational animals have imagination without possessing rational discourse (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 41–43). Heidegger, interpreting Aristotle's broader framework, emphasizes that λόγος—"speaking"—is "to exhibit beings in themselves, if this speaking is of such a character that it shows beings in their having-of-limits" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 43); doxa, as a mode of λόγος, thus requires the discursive articulation that phantasia by itself does not provide. Nevertheless, phantasia furnishes the representational ground upon which doxa operates, for without the phantasma there would be nothing for the soul to judge as true or false. The voluntariness of deliberative phantasia further distinguishes it from doxa: one can summon an image at will, as when one places things before the eyes in rhetorical practice (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 5), whereas belief is constrained by what appears to be the case. Caston accordingly identifies phantasia as the locus of a distinctive form of intentionality—one that makes error possible precisely because its content need not correspond to what is actually perceived (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, p. 18). The full treatment of phantasia's relation to πάθος, to habituated imagination, and to ὄρεξις will be developed in subsequent chapters, where the affective and appetitive dimensions of practical reasoning come into sharper focus.
